lesson.body:
When you smell a wine, just pick which broad family feels closest. The main ones are fruit (red like cherry, black like blackberry, citrus, stone like peach, tropical like pineapple), floral (roses), herbal or vegetal (cut grass, bell pepper, mint), spice (pepper, clove), and earth or mineral (wet soil, stone, mushroom).

One more family points to oak. Notes of vanilla, toast, coffee, or smoke usually come from new, heavily toasted oak — and increasingly from oak chips or staves dropped into a tank, not just from barrels or long aging. Spotting them tells you oak was involved, though smoke can also come from the grape or winemaking.

For everyday descriptors, guess freely: if a wine recalls your grandmother's jam, that counts. The exception is faults — wet cardboard, vinegar, nail polish, or rotten egg. Those aren't personal impressions; they're signs something went wrong, and learning to catch them is part of the skill.
outcomes: Sort a wine's smell into a broad family
Spot the notes that point to oak
Tell a personal impression from a wine fault

deep_notes: The best-known wine aroma wheel was designed in the 1980s by Ann Noble, a sensory scientist at the University of California, Davis. It works from the centre outwards: broad families in the middle, narrower groups in the next ring, and specific notes on the outside. Starting broad works because saying 'fruit' is far easier than saying 'raspberry'. Once you have the family, the exact note is a much smaller guess.

Barrel makers, called coopers, toast the inside of each barrel over a fire. The heat breaks down parts of the wood and releases vanillin, the same compound that gives vanilla pods their smell. A barrel gives most flavour when new. After a few fills it gives very little, and winemakers call it neutral oak. Chips and staves are popular because they give oak flavour faster and far more cheaply than new barrels.

Smell is closely wired to memory. Signals from your nose travel very directly to the parts of the brain that handle emotion and memory, which is why a scent can bring back a place or a person in a flash. This is often called the Proust effect, after a French novelist who wrote about a cake dipped in tea bringing back his childhood. A personal memory is often the quickest route to a name: grandmother's jam might lead you to cooked strawberry.

Each fault smell has a cause. Wet cardboard or a musty cellar smell usually means cork taint, from a compound called TCA. Vinegar points to volatile acidity, meaning too much acetic acid, the acid in vinegar: bacteria, helped by air, make it from some of the alcohol. The nail polish smell comes from ethyl acetate, which often appears alongside it. Rotten egg is hydrogen sulphide, a gas yeast can make when it is stressed, for example when it runs short of nutrients.

deeper.body: The musty, wet-cardboard smell of cork taint comes from a compound called TCA. People can notice it in astonishingly tiny amounts, just a few parts per trillion. A mild case may not smell musty at all. It simply flattens the fruit, so the wine seems dull and closed. Screw caps rule out the cork itself, although TCA can occasionally come from a winery's wood or cellar.
deeper.title: Cork taint up close

opts: Flatten the fruit so it seems dull
deeper.q: What can a mild case of cork taint do to a wine?
deeper.why: A mild case may not smell musty at all. It just dulls the fruit, which makes it easy to miss.

deeper.body: Not every off smell is clear-cut. Brettanomyces, or 'Brett', is a wild yeast that can give barnyard, leather or sticking-plaster smells. A trace can add an earthy, savoury edge that some drinkers enjoy. A lot of it buries the fruit, and most tasters then call it a fault. With Brett, where the line falls is partly a matter of taste.
deeper.title: Brett, the grey area

deeper.q: Which of these smells can come from Brett?
deeper.why: Brett, a wild yeast, gives barnyard, leather and sticking-plaster smells. Lemon is a fruit note and rose is a floral note, and Brett gives neither.

deeper.body: Where the oak grew changes the flavour. American oak tends to give bold vanilla and coconut, a classic mark of traditional Rioja. French oak is usually subtler, adding spice and a finer texture. The toast level matters too: a light toast keeps more of the wood's own character, while a heavy toast leans towards coffee, smoke and roasted notes.

deeper.q: French oak usually gives a wine bolder coconut notes than American oak.
deeper.why: It is the other way round. American oak is known for bold vanilla and coconut, while French oak is subtler and spicier.

v2.body:
In 1984 **Ann Noble**, a scientist at the University of California, Davis, published a tool for naming smells, or aromas. Tasting notes were full of words like 'elegant' and 'harmonious', which say nothing about the smell. Noble chose plain, shared words and set them on a circle: the **Wine Aroma Wheel**. Her practice tip: add a little real lemon, vanilla or clove to a plain wine.

The wheel has three rings: broad **families** in the middle, narrower groups next, single notes outside. Start in the middle, because saying 'fruit' is far easier than saying 'raspberry'. Then step outwards: fruit, berry, raspberry. Stuck? Stop at the family. 'Fruity and a bit spicy' is already a useful note.

Most wine smells fall into five families: fruit; floral, like roses; herbal or vegetal, like cut grass, bell pepper or mint; spice, like pepper or clove; and earth or mineral, like wet soil, stone or mushroom. Wine courses often split fruit, the biggest family, into groups. Red wines lean towards red fruit (cherry, strawberry, raspberry) and black fruit (blackberry, blackcurrant, black plum). Whites lean towards green fruit (apple, pear), citrus (lemon, lime, grapefruit), stone fruit (peach, apricot) and tropical fruit (pineapple, mango). Red fruit often smells brighter and tangier, black fruit darker and riper.

Some smells come from the barrel, not the grape. Vanilla, toast, coffee and smoke usually point to new **oak** barrels: barrel insides are toasted over a fire. A new barrel gives the most flavour; after a few uses, very little. Oak chips or staves (wooden planks) in a tank give these notes too, faster and more cheaply. But smoke can also come from the grape or the winemaking.

A **descriptor** is any word you use for a smell. For everyday descriptors, guess freely. Smell is closely tied to memory: if a wine brings back your grandmother's jam, that counts, and it can lead you to a name.

The exception is **faults**, flaws in the wine. They are not personal impressions but signs something went wrong:

• Wet cardboard or a musty cellar: **cork taint**, a 'corked' wine
• Vinegar: bacteria turned some alcohol into acetic acid, vinegar's acid
• Nail polish: a sharp, chemical smell that often comes with vinegar
• Rotten egg: a sulphur gas made by stressed yeast, the tiny living things that make wine

Wet soil, mushroom and forest floor are earthy notes, part of a wine's character. Wet cardboard is a fault, and a mild case of cork taint may not smell musty at all: the fruit just seems dull. In a restaurant, the small taste you are poured is your chance to check for faults. Not liking a wine is not a fault.
deep_notes: The scientist was Ann Noble. She joined the University of California, Davis, in 1974, the first woman hired to teach in its department of grape growing and winemaking. Her wheel first appeared in 1984 and was refined in 1987. She left out words that judge a wine, such as 'harmonious', and kept words for things you can actually smell. Her advice was hands-on: add a real food, such as citrus, apricot or clove, to a plain wine and learn each smell.

The rings work like a family tree. The original wheel's centre holds about a dozen broad families, with narrower groups in the middle ring and specific notes on the outside. Some of its central families are not pleasant at all, such as chemical, oxidised (spoiled by air) and microbiological (caused by bacteria or yeast). The wheel was built to describe faults as well as fine smells. Starting broad works because naming a family is easy, and from there the exact note is a much smaller guess.

Some notes have a known chemical cause. The green bell pepper smell in Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc comes from compounds called methoxypyrazines, which we can notice at around 2 parts per trillion in water or white wine. Levels fall as grapes ripen and sunlight keeps them down, so they show most in cooler places. The black pepper note in some Syrah has a known cause too: rotundone, a key part of the smell of black peppercorns.

Fruit words also hint at ripeness. Fresh, tart fruit, like sour cherry or green apple, often points to a cooler place or an earlier harvest, while jammy or baked fruit suggests heat and very ripe grapes. Some grapes have a signature fruit: blackcurrant is so typical of Cabernet Sauvignon that it shows up in its wines almost wherever they are made. Learning a grape's signature turns a fruit note into a clue.

Barrel makers, called coopers, bend the oak planks over a fire, and that heat also toasts the inside of the barrel. Heating breaks down parts of the wood and releases vanillin, the same substance that gives vanilla pods their smell. A barrel gives most flavour when new. After a few uses it gives very little, and winemakers call it neutral oak. Chips and staves are popular because they give oak flavour faster and far more cheaply than new barrels.

Smell is closely wired to memory. Signals from your nose travel very directly to the parts of the brain that handle emotion and memory, which is why a scent can bring back a place or a person in a flash. This is often called the Proust effect, after a French novelist who wrote about a cake dipped in tea bringing back his childhood. A personal memory is often the quickest route to a name: grandmother's jam might lead you to cooked strawberry.

Each fault smell has a cause. Wet cardboard or a musty cellar smell usually means cork taint, from a compound called TCA. Vinegar points to volatile acidity, meaning too much acetic acid: bacteria, helped by air, make it from some of the alcohol. The nail polish smell comes from ethyl acetate, which often appears alongside it. Rotten egg is hydrogen sulphide, a gas yeast can make when it is stressed, for example when it runs short of nutrients.

Another common fault is oxidation, when a wine has had too much air. A white turns a deeper yellow or even brownish, and the fresh fruit gives way to flat smells of bruised apple, cooked fruit or nuts. It is easy to confuse with age, because old wines also lose their bright fruit. In a restaurant, sniff the wine itself, not the cork: a musty cork does not prove the wine is corked.

deeper.body: The musty, wet-cardboard smell of cork taint comes from a compound called TCA. People can notice it in astonishingly tiny amounts, just a few parts per trillion. A mild case may not smell musty at all: a 2013 study in Japan suggests TCA partly works by dulling the smell-sensing cells in your nose, so the fruit simply seems flat. Screw caps rule out the cork itself, although TCA can occasionally come from a winery's wood or cellar.
deeper.title: Cork taint up close

deeper.key: A mild case of cork taint may not smell musty; it just flattens the fruit.
opts: Flatten the fruit so it seems dull
deeper.q: What can a mild case of cork taint do to a wine?
deeper.remember: Flat, dull fruit can be a quiet cork.
deeper.why: TCA can dull your sense of smell itself, which makes a mild case easy to miss.

deeper.body: Not every off smell is clear-cut. Brettanomyces, or 'Brett', is a wild yeast that can give barnyard, leather or sticking-plaster smells. A trace can add an earthy, savoury edge that some drinkers and winemakers accept, even enjoy. A lot of it buries the fruit, and most tasters then call it a fault. With Brett, where the line falls is partly a matter of taste.
deeper.title: Brett, the grey area

deeper.key: Brett, a wild yeast, gives barnyard, leather and sticking-plaster smells.
deeper.q: Which of these smells can come from Brett?
deeper.why: A trace can add a savoury edge, but a lot buries the fruit, so the dose decides fault or feature.

deeper.body: Where the oak grew changes the flavour. American oak holds more of the substances behind coconut and sweet vanilla notes, a classic mark of traditional Rioja, a Spanish red. French oak is usually subtler, adding spice and a finer texture. The toast level matters too: a light toast keeps more of the wood's own character, while a heavy toast leans towards coffee, smoke and roasted notes, and even tames American oak's coconut.
deeper.title: American or French oak

deeper.key: American oak gives bold coconut and vanilla; French oak is subtler and spicier.
deeper.q: French oak usually gives a wine bolder coconut notes than American oak.
deeper.why: So a strong coconut note in a red, like traditional Rioja, often points to American oak.
